caption_hook: The Granite State has also been a drifting microcontinent, a mountain belt and an ice sheet's dumping ground.

layers.name: MADISON BOULDER
layers.hook: A boulder bigger than a house
layers.what: The retreating ice sheet carried huge blocks of granite and dropped them far from where they were torn loose. Madison Boulder is one of the largest of these glacial erratics in North America.
layers.bonus: It is roughly 83 feet long and is estimated to weigh about 5,000 tons.

layers.name: CONWAY GRANITE
layers.what: Magma rose through the crust and cooled slowly underground into coarse pink-gray granite. Ice and weather have since exposed it as the sheer cliffs around North Conway.
layers.bonus: Cathedral Ledge, a cliff about 700 feet high, is a favorite of rock climbers.

layers.name: CONCORD GRANITE
layers.what: Hot magma cooled underground into light-gray granite with a fine, even grain. Quarried in Concord from the 1800s, it was cut into blocks used for grand public buildings.
layers.bonus: The State House in Concord, finished in 1819, is built of granite from nearby Rattlesnake Hill.

layers.name: LITTLETON FORMATION
layers.what: Ocean mud and sand were buried, folded and baked into hard schist and quartzite when a small continent crashed into North America. That tough rock outlasted the softer land around it.
layers.bonus: Mount Monadnock gave its name to any lone mountain left standing by erosion.

layers.name: MASSABESIC GNEISS
layers.what: In the southeast, the oldest bedrock belongs to Avalonia, a strip of crust that broke from the edge of an ancient supercontinent. It drifted and then docked onto North America.
layers.bonus: Lake Massabesic, which supplies Manchester's drinking water, sits on it.
